newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM remark not seen altering investors stance.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM remark not seen altering investors stance.

text.p: Japanese institutional investors do not plan to cut their U.S. Treasury holdings despite Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's comment that Japan might be tempted to sell some of its U.S. Treasuries, fund managers said on Tuesday.

"I hope the U.S. will engage in efforts and in cooperation to maintain exchange stability so we will not succumb to the temptation to sell off Treasury bills and switch our funds to gold," Hashimoto said, in response to a question after a speech in New York on Monday. Japan's Finance Ministry later said he had been misunderstood.

"Few people took Hashimoto's remarks (on Treasuries) seriously. Nevertheless, Treasuries fell half a point as the comments come amid a growing effort by Japanese banks to shrink their operations in New York," said a senior U.S. Treasury bond trader at a major U.S. brokerage in Tokyo.

It would be difficult for the Japanese government to make a political decision to sell large amounts of U.S. Treasuries, the trader said, but the Japanese private sector may not be so hesitant if global business strategies call for such a move.
Traders said many Japanese financial institutions are already shrinking their U.S. assets, including Treasuries, as part of a gradual shrinking of their overseas operations.

Japanese banks have been cutting back on their New York operations since Daiwa Bank's branch there revealed massive losses two years ago that resulted in stricter inspections of Japanese banks by the Federal Reserve, the bond trader said.
The banks have been slowly reducing assets, including outstanding loans to companies, particularly unlisted ones, and securities such as U.S. Treasuries, he said.

The prime minister's comments rocked financial markets in New York, weighing down U.S. Treasury bonds, pushing the dollar below 115 yen and hammering down the Dow Jones industrial average by 192.25 points to 7,604.26.
Later, Japan's Finance Ministry issued a statement saying Hashimoto had been misunderstood, and that the prime minister regretted his intentions had not been accurately conveyed.

In Tokyo, Treasury prices recovered on buying to cover their positions and bargain-hunting by Japanese investors, and fund managers at cash-rich life insurance firms said they had no plans to change their foreign investment plans.

Many Japanese institutional investors are still diversifying their portfolios to increase their foreign bond investments as the interest rate gap between Japan and other countries, including the United States, remains wide.

Tokyo traders said they did not believe that the Japanese government would actually unload its Treasury holdings, part of the world's largest external reserves, which totalled $221.761 billion as of the end of May.
"We are not thinking of altering our foreign investment strategy after the prime minister's remarks," said Shingo Uchiyama, a manager at Dai-Ichi Mutual Life Insurance Co.
"People may have used Mr Hashimoto's comments as an excuse to sell off Treasuries and U.S. stocks overnight," he said.
According to the Life Insurance Association of Japan, life insurers held about 17.10 trillion yen ($150 billion) worth of foreign securities as of the end of February.
"Investors will not change their asset allocations because of his comments," said Koshi Watanabe, manager of foreign investment at Chiyoda Mutual Life Insurance Co.
"Life insurance firms are still in the process of increasing their foreign bond holdings and I don't believe that trend has changed after Hashimoto's remarks," Watanabe said. ($1=114 yen)
